profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between two legal workstreams preparing a comparative legal-policy briefing for a university-affiliated policy center and its external advisors on institutional options for sub-regional cooperation between Fujian and Taiwan, using the Pingtan Experimental Area as the case study. The immediate context is that the mainland-law workstream and the Taiwan-law comparative workstream have each drafted portions of a memo on urban planning system coordination, but they need to align interfaces before a steering-group circulation later in the week. The agenda is to confirm what goes into the 'legal aspects' section, how to map planning tiers across the two systems, which shared artifact is the live master for edits, and what standard counts as 'ready for circulation.' The expected outcome is apparent agreement on handoffs, artifact ownership, and section boundaries for the comparative memo and annexed comparison table.

members.name: Li Wen
members.role: Senior Associate, PRC Administrative and Land-Use Law
members.expertise: Mainland China urban-rural planning law, administrative approvals, special development zones, regulatory drafting
members.background: Beijing-based lawyer who has advised local governments and state-linked developers on planning approvals and pilot-zone compliance; he is leading the mainland-law chapter and consolidating the final memo.
members.private_state: He wants a clean, defensible draft that will not overstate what is legally binding in mainland practice, and he is trying to keep the memo compact enough to circulate internally without triggering another round of structural edits.
hidden_assumptions: If a planning term is used without qualification in the memo, it should default to the mainland statutory meaning used in PRC urban-rural planning practice.

The 'legal aspects' section should include binding laws, regulations, and formal approval bases, while softer policy guidance or administrative practice belongs only in background notes if mentioned at all.
Because the final deliverable is a narrative memo, the Word draft is the operative master document and any 'redline' should be made there.
A draft is 'ready for circulation' once the structure is settled and the legal propositions are directionally correct, even if some citation formatting or bilingual polishing remains.

members.name: Chen Yu-Hsuan
members.role: Comparative Legal Consultant, Taiwan Urban Governance
members.expertise: Taiwan spatial planning law, cross-strait institutional comparison, bilingual legal synthesis, administrative procedure
members.background: Taipei-trained legal researcher with experience on comparative governance projects involving planning institutions, land-use controls, and public administration; she is responsible for the Taiwan-side mapping and the comparative matrix.
members.private_state: She wants the memo to be credible to cross-strait academic and policy readers, which for her requires functional comparability, careful bilingual citation, and inclusion of the practical review mechanisms that shape how planning systems actually operate.
hidden_assumptions: Comparative drafting should map institutions by function, so shared labels like 'detailed planning' can legitimately cover non-identical lower-tier plans if they play a similar implementation role.

In a cross-strait comparison, the 'legal aspects' section naturally includes policy directives, implementing opinions, and established review practices because those are part of the operative legal-administrative environment.
The comparison matrix in Excel is the source-of-truth artifact from which the narrative memo is later populated, so a request to 'redline the matrix' means annotating that spreadsheet.
A draft is only 'ready for circulation' when it is safe for a mixed external steering audience to read, meaning citations, translations, and cross-references are already cleaned up.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss strengthening the connection between 'master plan and detailed planning.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the mainland PRC statutory category of control detailed planning and its formal relationship to the master/overall planning hierarchy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the broader implementation-level planning layer on the Taiwan side that is functionally downstream from higher-level plans, even if it is not the same legal category.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes directly from the project topic and sounds standard to both of them, so each assumes the other is using it in the obvious comparative sense without needing to restate the legal taxonomy behind it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to cover the 'legal aspects' relevant to joint planning, development, and management in Pingtan.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this section should be limited to binding legal instruments and formal approval documents, with softer materials excluded or relegated to background.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this section should also cover pilot policy documents, implementing opinions, and review practices because those shape actual administrative cooperation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal-policy work, both binding law and quasi-legal implementation materials are routinely discussed together, so the phrase 'legal aspects' sounds sufficiently precise while hiding a boundary difference neither thinks needs unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'redline the comparison matrix'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that M2 will 'redline the comparison matrix' before M1 consolidates the draft.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects tracked changes and comments in the Word annex or memo table that he will directly merge into the final draft.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to annotate the Excel comparison spreadsheet, adding source columns and comments there as the master comparative artifact.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams have been using both a Word memo and a spreadsheet table, and 'matrix' plus 'redline' feels like ordinary coordination shorthand, so neither pauses to specify file type or edit method.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the draft should be 'ready for circulation' after the next round of edits.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means ready for internal steering-group review once the argument structure is stable, even if some bilingual citations and formatting remain provisional.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means ready for a broader mixed audience, with citations checked, translations harmonized, and no obvious placeholders left.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In professional settings, 'circulation' often refers generically to the next distribution step, and because both intend to share the draft soon, the phrase creates a false sense of alignment on quality threshold.
